**Why hybrid wins:** adding keyword matching catches the exact code directly, while vector search keeps handling the meaning of the rest of the query.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that an embedding sees E-4021 as similar to E-4012 goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it. The answer is about 185 words.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Sorting that many scores takes too long”?
check:1:1.a:
"Sorting that many scores takes too long" points at the wrong problem.

Sorting is not the slow part. A search returns a short list, maybe 10 results from each side. Sorting 20 numbers is instant. And reciprocal rank fusion sorts at the end too. It sorts the fused totals from highest to lowest. So avoiding sorting can't be the reason.

What the option misses is what the numbers mean. A BM25 score of 12 comes from word rarity and chunk length. It has no fixed top value. A vector score of 0.83 measures how close two embeddings are, usually on a scale near 0 to 1. The two numbers are on different scales, like comparing degrees to kilograms. If you sorted them together, keyword results would almost always win just because their numbers are bigger. That says nothing about which result is actually better.

That's why fusion uses each document's place in its own list. A place means the same thing in every list.

"The two kinds of score can't be compared" is better because it names the real issue: the scores are on different scales, so sorting them together gives a meaningless order.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Vector scores are always more accurate”?
check:1:2.a:
"Vector scores are always more accurate" is a tempting answer, but it doesn't fit the question.

**What it gets right:** vector search is good at meaning. It can match "payment failed" to "checkout error" even when the words differ.

**What it misses:** two things.

First, vector search isn't always better. Keyword search wins on exact terms. For a query like `error E-4021 on checkout`, BM25 (the classic keyword scoring formula) can find the chunk with that exact code. Vector search might return chunks that are only *about* checkout errors in general. That's why hybrid search runs both.

Second, accuracy isn't the real issue. The question is why you can't sort 12 and 0.83 together. Even if vector search were more accurate, its scores still live on a different scale. A BM25 score has no fixed top. A vector score is a similarity, often between 0 and 1. So 12 isn't "better" than 0.83. They're measuring different things.

**Why "The two kinds of score can't be compared" is right:** it names the real problem, which is mismatched scales. That's exactly why rank fusion merges by place in each list instead of by raw score.

judge.notes: The claims about BM25 having no fixed top and vector scores often falling between 0 and 1 go beyond the lesson but are true and consistent with it. The closing part runs to two sentences instead of the one requested, which is a minor issue.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Doc B, because 1st place wins”?
check:2:0.a:
"Doc B, because 1st place wins" gets one thing right. Doc B did earn a top spot, and in rank fusion a higher place does give more points. So Doc B is not ignored. It still collects points from the vector list.

What it misses is that rank fusion **adds up** points from every list. It does not pick a winner from a single list. Doc B shows up in only one list, so it gets points only once. Doc A shows up in both, so it gets points twice.

Rank fusion also adds a fixed number to every place before working out the points. That keeps the gap between 1st and 2nd small. So Doc A's 2nd place in vector search is worth almost as much as Doc B's 1st place. On top of that, Doc A gets a full 1st-place share from keyword search, which Doc B never gets.

Put simply: two nearly-top finishes beat one top finish.

"Doc A, as both lists give it points" is better because rank fusion rewards documents that both searches agree on, and Doc A collects points from both lists while Doc B collects from only one.

check:2:2.q: Why not “They tie, as both reach 1st place”?
check:2:2.a:
It's a fair guess. Both documents do reach 1st place somewhere: Doc A in keyword search, Doc B in vector search. So on "best place" alone, they look even.

But rank fusion doesn't look only at a document's best place. It gives a document points from **every** list it shows up in, and then adds those points together.

Doc A appears in both lists. It gets points for 1st in keyword search, and more points for 2nd in vector search. Two helpings of points.

Doc B appears in only one list. It gets points for 1st in vector search, and nothing from keyword search, because it's missing there. One helping.

Second place still earns a good share of points. A fixed number is added to every place, so 1st doesn't count far more than 2nd. That means Doc A's two helpings add up to more than Doc B's single one.

The option gets "both reach 1st" right. It misses that fusion adds up points across lists.

"Doc A, as both lists give it points" is better because rank fusion rewards being found by both searches, not just placing first in one.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only slight wobble is "more points for 2nd in vector search", which could be read as 2nd earning more than 1st, though it means additional points.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

**Exact terms get lost.** A search for `E-4021` returns chunks about checkout in general, but not the one naming that code. That hints only vector search is running.

**Meaning gets lost.** A question worded differently from the docs finds nothing useful. That hints only keyword search is running.

**One search always wins.** The fused list keeps ignoring strong hits from one search. That often means raw scores were added instead of places. The two searches score on different scales, so the bigger numbers drown out the smaller ones.

**Tests look good, then results drop in real use.** If test questions copy the docs' wording, a broken merge can look fine. Then real users type error codes or rephrase things, and quality falls.

**Quickest check**

Pick one query and look at both input lists next to the fused list. Ask two questions:

- Does a document near the top of both lists land at or near the top?
- Does a document found by only one search still appear, lower down?

The lesson's example shows this. `d1` is high in both lists, so it comes first. `d7` and `d9` were each found once, and they still make the list.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the simple "add up points by place" rule needs extra care.

**One search is much weaker for your questions.** Reciprocal rank fusion treats both lists as equally trustworthy. If your users mostly type exact error codes, the vector list may pull in loosely related chunks and push good ones down. Test on real questions, then give the stronger list more weight, or send code-like queries to keyword search alone.

**Confidence gets thrown away.** Using place instead of score means a perfect match and a barely relevant one at the same place get the same points. When precision really matters, add a **reranker**: a model that reads the question and each top chunk together and rescores them.

**The lists are cut too short.** A document missing from one list gets nothing from that list. If each search returns only 10 results, a good chunk ranked 11th in one list loses out. Fetch more candidates from each search, say 50, fuse them, then keep the top 10.

learn:term.a:
**TF-IDF** stands for "term frequency, inverse document frequency." It scores how well a chunk of text matches the words in a query.

Picture searching a pile of letters for one about your order. The word "the" is in every letter, so it tells you nothing. A code like "E-4021" appears in only a few, so a letter containing it is likely the one you want. TF-IDF works the same way. A word counts more when it is rare across all the documents (the "inverse document frequency" part). It also counts more each time it repeats inside a chunk (the "term frequency" part).

The lesson calls it BM25's older, simpler cousin. Both favour rare words. In TF-IDF, every repeat keeps adding to the score. BM25 stops adding after a few. TF-IDF also evens out chunk length more crudely.

In the example, the keyword list `d3, d1, d7` is the kind of ranking a keyword scorer produces. A scorer like TF-IDF or BM25 decides that order. The lesson also names TF-IDF as a free baseline: an embedding model that cannot beat it is not earning its cost.

judge.notes: No real problems. The only soft spot is the last paragraph, which links TF-IDF to the example's keyword list even though the lesson says that list is scored with BM25; the 'a scorer like' wording keeps it hedged.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The table has no embeddings column yet”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair guess. The lesson does say every index needs **embeddings**, the lists of numbers that capture meaning. So the option is right that embeddings matter.

But a Delta Sync index does not need an embeddings column in your table. You can use **managed embeddings**. You name an embedding model endpoint, such as `databricks-gte-large-en`, and point `embedding_source_column` at your text column. Databricks then makes the embeddings for you. That is exactly what the lesson's own example does with a table that has "no embeddings yet."

So a missing embeddings column is a normal starting point, not a reason for failure. It only matters if you chose **self-managed embeddings**, where you bring your own column. The question doesn't say you did.

"Change Data Feed is not turned on for the source table" is the better answer. The lesson names it as a specific requirement for this exact setup, a Delta Sync index on a Standard endpoint. Change Data Feed is the table setting that logs which rows changed, so the index can update only those.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The table has too few rows to index”?
check:0:2.a:
It is a fair guess in one way. It points at the source table, and that is the right place to look. A Delta Sync index follows a Delta table (a Databricks table), so problems with that table can stop the index.

But row count is not a rule the lesson gives. Nothing says a table needs a minimum number of rows. The lesson's own example plans for 200,000 chunks, and nothing suggests a smaller table would be refused. Size matters for a different choice: which endpoint type to pick. Around 10 million vectors, storage-optimized becomes the better fit. Being small is not a reason to fail.

The question names a specific setup: a Delta Sync index on a Standard endpoint. The lesson gives one firm requirement for exactly that pairing. The table must have Change Data Feed turned on. That setting keeps a log of which rows changed, so the index only updates those rows.

"Change Data Feed is not turned on" is better because it is the one requirement the lesson states for a Delta Sync index on a Standard endpoint.

check:1:1.a:
"Continuous, always streaming" is not wrong in what it does. It would keep the index up to date within moments of every change. Your help-desk answers would never be stale.

The problem is that this question doesn't need that speed. The documents change only a few times a day, and answers can be a day behind. Continuous mode keeps a streaming job running all the time. A streaming job is a process that keeps watching the table for new changes. Here it would sit idle most of the day, and you would still pay for it. That is why Continuous costs more.

The lesson's rule is to pick Continuous only when data must be fresh within about 5 minutes. A day of delay is far from that.

"Triggered, synced once a day" is better because it meets the day-behind need with the cheapest sync mode. The index updates only when you call `index.sync()`. The endpoint itself still bills for every hour it is up, whichever sync mode you choose.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Either, they cost the same”?
check:1:2.a:
"Either, they cost the same" gets one thing right. Both sync modes would keep this index fresh enough. Continuous updates within moments. Triggered updates when you call `sync()`. A day of delay is allowed, so neither mode would give stale answers.

What it misses is the cost. The two modes do not cost the same.

**Continuous** keeps a streaming job running all the time. A streaming job is a process that never stops, always watching the table for changes. You pay for it around the clock, even when nothing has changed. Your documents only change a few times a day, so most of that time is wasted.

**Triggered** only updates when you call sync. The lesson calls it the cheapest mode. You get the freshness you need without paying for a job that is always on.

The general rule: choose Continuous only when the data must be fresh within minutes. That is not the case here.

**Why "Triggered, synced once a day" is better:** a day-old index is fine for this help desk, so the cheapest mode that meets that need is the right one.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Change Data Feed on the table”?
check:2:0.a:
Change Data Feed is a real setting from this lesson, so it is easy to reach for. It keeps a log of which rows in a table changed. On a Standard endpoint, a Delta Sync index needs it so it can update only those rows.

But that is about keeping the index **up to date**. It is not about **who may search** it. If Change Data Feed were off, the index would fail to set up or sync. It would not refuse one person's search while letting others in. Ana's problem is permission, not freshness.

Look at what she has. `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` let her reach the place where the index lives in Unity Catalog. `CAN_USE` is an endpoint permission. It lets her create an index on that endpoint, but searching needs nothing on the endpoint. So `CAN_USE` does not help her search at all.

**"SELECT on the index"** is better because it is the one search permission she is missing: searching needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the index, and she has only the first two.

check:2:1.a:
It is a fair guess. Ana's search is refused, and `CAN_MANAGE` is the strongest permission on the endpoint. So it seems like more power should fix it.

But the endpoint is the wrong place to look. Searching an index needs nothing on the endpoint at all. Endpoint permissions are only for building on the endpoint:

- `CAN_USE` lets you create an index on it.
- `CAN_MANAGE` lets you delete the endpoint or change who may use it.

Neither one lets you read what is inside an index. Giving Ana `CAN_MANAGE` would let her delete the endpoint, but her search would still be refused.

Search permission lives in Unity Catalog, Databricks' catalog of data and who may use it. The index is an object there, with a three-part name like `main.support.docs_index`. To search it, you need `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, and `SELECT` on the index itself. Ana already has the first two. Her `CAN_USE` is fine, but it does not help with searching.

"`SELECT` on the index" is better because it is the one Unity Catalog permission she still lacks, and it is exactly what reading the index requires.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Stale answers.** You add rows to the table, but search never returns them. A Triggered index only updates when `sync()` is called. If nobody calls it, the index quietly falls behind.
- **Creation fails on a Standard endpoint.** A Delta Sync index there needs Change Data Feed on its table. If it is off, the setup stops with an error.
- **A bill with no traffic.** Costs keep coming in every hour, even when nobody searches. An unused endpoint still holds an index.
- **Cost higher than it needs to be.** Continuous sync runs a streaming job all the time. If data an hour old is fine, you are paying for freshness you don't use. Tens of millions of vectors on Standard is the same kind of overspend.
- **Permission errors on search.** These usually mean missing USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA or SELECT on the index.

**Quickest check**

Add one test row and run a search for it. Then sync, and search again. If it only shows up after the sync, the index works but needs regular syncing.

Then read your setup against the four questions, in order.

learn:stops.a:
The fixed order of rules is a good default. Here are three places where it needs extra care.

**Your data sits right around 10 million vectors.** The cutoff is a rough guide, not a hard wall. If your app needs answers in tens of milliseconds (thousandths of a second), Standard may still be worth its higher cost, even past 10 million.

**Your data must be fresh, but you are on storage-optimized.** Storage-optimized endpoints only do Triggered sync, so Continuous is off the table. Schedule syncs often, or move to a Standard endpoint if freshness matters more than cost.

**You change your embedding model.** Vectors from different models do not match, so old chunks and new questions stop lining up. Re-embed every chunk and rebuild the index. With self-managed embeddings, also make sure your questions are embedded by that same model.

judge.notes: No real problems. The embedding-model point goes beyond what the lesson states, but it does not contradict it.

learn:term.a:
Think of the index at the back of a textbook. The book holds everything. The index is a separate list, built so you can find things fast.

Here, an **index** is a searchable copy of your text chunks. Each chunk is stored with its **embedding**: a list of numbers that captures its meaning. That lets a search find chunks that mean something close to your question, not just ones with the same words.

The index sits on an **endpoint**: the machines kept running to answer searches. The index is the data. The endpoint is what serves it.

In the example, `create_delta_sync_index` builds an index called `main.support.docs_index`. Its source is `main.support.doc_chunks`, which is a **Delta table**: Databricks' standard kind of table, with rows and columns.

Both names have three parts because they live in **Unity Catalog**. That is Databricks' central list of data and who may use it. The three parts are catalog, schema (a folder-like group) and name.

Finally, `index.sync()` pulls the latest table changes into the index.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only small stretch is saying the source table also lives in Unity Catalog and is Databricks' 'standard' table type, which the lesson only implies.

check:0:1.a:
"Passage B, at 0.10" mixes up which way the score runs.

**What it gets right:** it reads the two scores correctly. B really does score 0.10. And with some measures, like plain distance between two places, a smaller number does mean closer. So picking the low number is a natural guess.

**What it misses:** cosine similarity runs the other way. It measures whether two vectors (lists of numbers) point the same direction.

- **1** means they point the same way, so the meanings are very close.
- **0** means they are unrelated.

So 0.10 says passage B is almost unrelated to the question. In the lesson's example, "expense claim" scored 0.12 against "parental leave". That is about how far off B is. Sending B to the LLM (the language model that writes the answer) would give it text that has little to do with the question. Search ranks passages by cosine from highest to lowest, so B would land near the bottom.

**Why A is better:** at 0.95, passage A points almost the same way as the question, so it most likely means nearly the same thing and can help answer it.

check:0:2.a:
"Neither: cosine measures length" has the idea backwards. Cosine similarity deliberately ignores length. It only asks which way two vectors point.

There is one small grain of truth in it. Length does show up in the calculation. You multiply the numbers position by position, add them up, then divide by the two vectors' lengths. But that division is there to *cancel* length out, not to measure it. What's left is purely about direction.

Picture two arrows on a map. One is short, one is long. If they point the same way, cosine says they match. That's why a short question can still match a long passage.

So the option misses the main point. A score of 0.95 is not a statement about size. It says the question and passage A point almost the same way. In embedding terms, that means they mean nearly the same thing. A score of 0.10 says passage B points somewhere nearly unrelated.

Passage A is the better answer because its cosine of 0.95 means its meaning lies very close to the question's, so it most likely holds what the question is asking about.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The newer model is broken”?
check:1:1.a:
It's a fair first guess. The results did get worse right after the switch, so blaming the new model feels natural. But that guess misses what actually went wrong.

The newer model is probably fine. If you embedded both your documents and your questions with it, search would likely work well, maybe even better than before.

The real problem is mixing. Each model learns its own space on its own. Nobody chose what each dimension means, so position 5 in the old model's vector has nothing to do with position 5 in the new one. The two models might not even give the same count of numbers.

So cosine similarity, which compares direction, is now comparing arrows drawn on two different maps. The scores come out as numbers, but they mean nothing. The "nearest" passage is just noise.

The fix shows it isn't a broken model. Re-embed all your documents with the new model, or keep using the old model for questions. Either way, everything lives in one space again.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it names the real cause: vectors are only comparable when the same model made them.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that models may give different vector lengths goes beyond the lesson but is hedged and true, and the answer is right at the edge of the ~200-word limit.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The documents got too long”?
check:1:2.a:
"The documents got too long" sounds reasonable, but it doesn't fit what happened.

First, the documents didn't change. The only thing that changed was the model used for the questions. If results were fine before the switch and nonsense after, the cause has to be the switch.

Second, length isn't what breaks search here. An embedding model gives the same count of numbers for any text, short or long. And cosine similarity compares direction, not length, so a long passage can still match a short question.

It does get one small thing right. Very long text can blur its meaning, and models have an input limit, so text past that point gets cut off. But that would make results slightly worse, not turn them into nonsense overnight.

The real issue is that each model learns its own space. Its dimensions (the positions in the list of numbers) mean different things. Comparing a vector from one model with a vector from another is like reading coordinates from two different maps.

"The two models' spaces don't match" is better because it points at the one thing that changed, and that change makes every comparison meaningless.

judge.notes: No real problems. The input-limit and 'blurred meaning' remarks are not in the lesson, but they are accurate and do not contradict it. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Yes: long passages always score low”?
check:2:1.a:
"Yes: long passages always score low" starts from a fair worry. A two-page passage has far more words than a two-line question, so it seems they shouldn't match well. Noticing that size gap is the only thing this option gets right.

What it misses is how the comparison works. Every text, short or long, becomes a list of 1,536 numbers. Picture that list as an arrow on a map. Cosine similarity only asks whether two arrows point the same way. The formula divides by each arrow's length, so how long an arrow is drops out of the score.

So a long passage is not pushed down for being long. The word "always" is also wrong. A long passage can score high or low depending on what it means.

In this case the score is 0.9. That is close to 1, which means "pointing the same way." It is a strong match, not a problem.

"No: cosine compares direction, not length" is better because it names the exact reason length can't drag the score down: cosine leaves length out by design.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Yes: the question must be longer”?
check:2:2.a:
"Yes: the question must be longer" starts from a fair worry. A two-line question and a two-page passage look very different, so it's natural to wonder whether they can match. That instinct is the one thing it gets right.

What it misses is how cosine similarity works. Each text becomes a vector, a list of numbers. Picture it as an arrow pointing somewhere in the embedding space. Cosine similarity only asks whether two arrows point the same way. 1 means the same direction, 0 means unrelated. The arrow's length doesn't count. When you divide the dot product by the two lengths, you remove length from the score on purpose. (The dot product means multiplying the numbers position by position and adding them up.)

The lesson also says that with `text-embedding-3-small`, a short text and a long one both come out as 1,536 numbers. So the question doesn't need to "catch up" in size. The 0.9 already tells you they point almost the same way, which means they're about the same thing.

"No: cosine compares direction, not length" is better because it names the actual reason the mismatch in size doesn't matter.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A score above 1.** Cosine tops out at 1, meaning "same direction". A bigger number means the step of dividing by the two vectors' lengths was skipped.
- **The longest passage keeps winning.** Without that division, long passages get big totals just for having bigger numbers, not for matching meaning. A short, exact answer loses to a long, rambling one.
- **Questions with internal terms come back with unrelated passages.** A product code the model never learned may land nowhere useful. Its nearest passage is just the least-bad guess, often with a low score.
- **The LLM answers confidently from the wrong passage.** The LLM answers from what retrieval returns. If the top passage is off, the answer is off.

**Quickest check**

Score a few pairs where you already know the answer, like the lesson's example. "Parental leave" vs "maternity leave" should score high, and vs "expense claim" should score near 0. Also score one text against itself: it should be exactly 1. Then try a short and a long passage that say the same thing. Both should score about the same against the question.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Words the model never learned.** Internal product codes, ticket numbers or team slang may land nowhere useful, so the right passage scores low. Add keyword search alongside it (often called **hybrid search**, meaning you combine exact-word matching with meaning matching).

**2. Switching embedding models.** Each model builds its own space, so a vector from one model means nothing next to a vector from another. If you upgrade the model, re-embed every passage, and always embed questions with the same model as the passages.

**3. A very large number of passages.** Comparing the question with every passage one by one is fine for hundreds, but gets slow for millions. Use a **vector index**, a structure that finds near neighbours without checking them all, such as Databricks Vector Search.

A related caution: "closest" is not always "correct." Text like "leave is allowed" and "leave is not allowed" can score very close. So return a few top passages, not just one, and let the LLM read them.

learn:term.a:
A **vector** is just the container. It's an ordered list of numbers, like `[0.12, -0.40, 0.88, ...]`. On its own it says nothing about meaning. A vector could hold anything: temperatures, prices, pixel colours.

An **embedding** is a vector made by a model from text, so that its position captures meaning. Every embedding is a vector, but not every vector is an embedding. "Embed" is also the verb: you embed a question to get its vector.

**An everyday comparison:** a vector is like a pair of map coordinates. Any two numbers make coordinates. An embedding is the coordinates of a real café, chosen so that similar cafés sit nearby.

**How they work together:** `text-embedding-3-small` embeds "parental leave" into a vector of 1,536 numbers. It does the same for "maternity leave." Because both are vectors, you can compare them with cosine similarity. That measures whether two arrows point the same way, ignoring their length. Here it gives 0.91, nearly the same direction. "Expense claim" scores 0.12, far off.

The model supplies the meaning. The vector gives you something you can do maths on.

judge.notes: Minor: the café analogy is loose ("chosen so similar cafés sit nearby"), and the lesson's example scores are presented as real model output.
